title: What do the key consumer configs do — `enable.auto.commit` (auto vs manual offset commit, and why manual + commit-after-processing gives at-least-once), `auto.offset.reset` (`earliest` vs `latest` when there is no committed offset), `max.poll.records` (max records per `poll()`, not a total cap), and `max.poll.interval.ms` (too-slow processing between polls triggers a rebalance)?
shortTitle: What do the key consumer configs do?

s1_definition.profdef: These four consumer settings control correctness, startup behaviour, and liveness. `enable.auto.commit` decides whether offsets commit automatically on a timer or whether you commit manually, and committing manually after processing gives clean at-least-once delivery. `auto.offset.reset` decides where a consumer starts when there is no committed offset, with `earliest` reading the whole backlog and `latest` skipping everything older than the moment it joins. `max.poll.records` caps how many records a single `poll()` returns, not a total limit. `max.poll.interval.ms` bounds the time allowed between successive `poll()` calls, so processing a batch too slowly triggers a rebalance.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a settlement clerk at National Bank of India. The auto-commit setting is whether the clerk marks slips cleared automatically on a timer or only after actually doing the work, and only-after-work is the safe habit. The offset-reset setting is, for a brand-new clerk with no record of where to start, whether they begin from the oldest slip in the tray or only from slips that arrive after they sit down. The max-poll-records setting is how many slips the clerk grabs in one handful. And the max-poll-interval setting is the rule that if the clerk takes too long before grabbing the next handful, the supervisor assumes they are stuck and reassigns their tray to someone else.
s1_definition.oneliner: enable.auto.commit controls safe manual commit for at-least-once, auto.offset.reset picks backlog versus skip for a fresh group, max.poll.records sizes each poll batch, and max.poll.interval.ms evicts a consumer that processes a batch too slowly.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** These four consumer settings control correctness, startup behaviour, and liveness. `enable.auto.commit` decides whether offsets commit automatically on a timer or whether you commit manually, and committing manually after processing gives clean at-least-once delivery. `auto.offset.reset` decides where a consumer starts when there is no committed offset, with `earliest` reading the whole backlog and `latest` skipping everything older than the moment it joins. `max.poll.records` caps how many records a single `poll()` returns, not a total limit. `max.poll.interval.ms` bounds the time allowed between successive `poll()` calls, so processing a batch too slowly triggers a rebalance.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a settlement clerk at National Bank of India. The auto-commit setting is whether the clerk marks slips cleared automatically on a timer or only after actually doing the work, and only-after-work is the safe habit. The offset-reset setting is, for a brand-new clerk with no record of where to start, whether they begin from the oldest slip in the tray or only from slips that arrive after they sit down. The max-poll-records setting is how many slips the clerk grabs in one handful. And the max-poll-interval setting is the rule that if the clerk takes too long before grabbing the next handful, the supervisor assumes they are stuck and reassigns their tray to someone else.

**One line to remember:** enable.auto.commit controls safe manual commit for at-least-once, auto.offset.reset picks backlog versus skip for a fresh group, max.poll.records sizes each poll batch, and max.poll.interval.ms evicts a consumer that processes a batch too slowly.

sections.s2_technical:
The `enable.auto.commit` setting, default true, makes the consumer commit the last polled offsets automatically every `auto.commit.interval.ms`, by default five seconds. The problem is that this timer is independent of whether you have finished processing, so auto-commit can advance the offset past records you have not yet handled. If you crash in that window, those records are skipped, which is message loss. To get clean at-least-once you set `props.put("enable.auto.commit", "false")` and call `consumer.commitSync()` only after a record or batch is fully processed. Because the commit follows processing, a crash before commit causes a reprocess, not a loss, and that is the defining at-least-once behaviour.

The `auto.offset.reset` setting decides where to start only when there is no valid committed offset for the group and partition, which happens for a brand-new group or when the committed offset has been deleted by retention. With `props.put("auto.offset.reset", "earliest")` the consumer starts at the oldest available record, so a new group reads the entire backlog, which you want for a system that must process all history. With `latest` the consumer starts at the end, so it only sees records produced after it joins and silently skips everything that already existed, which is a classic cause of a brand-new consumer appearing to receive nothing. The setting does nothing when a committed offset exists, because then the consumer simply resumes there.

The `max.poll.records` setting, default five hundred, caps how many records a single call to `poll()` returns. It is not a total limit on consumption and not a byte limit; it just shapes each batch. You tune it down, for example `props.put("max.poll.records", 50)`, when each record is expensive to process, so that you process and poll again frequently and do not blow the poll interval. You tune it up for lightweight records to improve throughput. The important misconception to avoid is thinking it limits total messages; it only limits per-poll batch size.

The `max.poll.interval.ms` setting, default five minutes, bounds the maximum time allowed between two successive `poll()` calls. The consumer must call `poll()` again within this window, because `poll()` is also how the consumer signals liveness for processing progress. If your handler takes longer than this to process a batch, the group coordinator assumes the consumer is stuck, removes it from the group, and triggers a rebalance that reassigns its partitions to others. This is why a slow message handler causes a rebalance even when heartbeats are still flowing: liveness of processing is separate from the heartbeat, and it is enforced by the poll interval. You fix a too-slow consumer by lowering `max.poll.records` so each batch is smaller, by speeding up processing, or by raising `max.poll.interval.ms` if the work genuinely takes longer.

A senior nuance is how these interact. Manual commit plus a right-sized `max.poll.records` plus a sane `max.poll.interval.ms` together give a consumer that is both safe and stable: it processes bounded batches, commits only after success, and does not get evicted mid-batch. Another nuance is that after a rebalance caused by a blown poll interval, the reassigned partitions may be reprocessed, so idempotency still matters. A final nuance is that `auto.offset.reset=none` throws if there is no committed offset, which you use when you want to fail loudly rather than guess where to start.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India deploys a new fraud-scoring consumer. The team must configure it so it processes the full transaction backlog, never loses a transaction, grabs a sensible batch size, and does not get kicked out of its group while scoring a heavy batch.

Problem 1 — the consumer must read all existing transactions, not just new ones. This is exactly what `auto.offset.reset=earliest` provides for a fresh group.

Problem 2 — a fraud transaction must never be silently skipped. This is exactly what disabling auto-commit and committing after scoring provides: clean at-least-once.

Problem 3 — scoring each record is slow, so grabbing five hundred at once takes too long and the group evicts the consumer, causing a rebalance. This is exactly what tuning `max.poll.records` down and respecting `max.poll.interval.ms` solves.

The code will show a fraud consumer with these four settings configured, processing bounded batches, committing only after scoring, and logging how the settings keep it correct and stable for Rajesh's and Priya's transactions.

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: broker1:9092
    consumer:
      group-id: fraud-scoring
      enable-auto-commit: false       # manual commit → at-least-once
      auto-offset-reset: earliest     # new group reads the whole backlog
      max-poll-records: 50            # small batch: scoring is expensive
      properties:
        max.poll.interval.ms: 300000  # 5 min: must poll again within this
      key-deserializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
      value-deserializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transactions topic with a large existing backlog, consumed by a brand-new fraud-scoring group.

Step 1 — because the group is new and there is no committed offset, `auto.offset.reset=earliest` makes the consumer start at the oldest record, so it reads the entire backlog rather than skipping it.

Step 2 — each `poll()` returns at most fifty records because `max.poll.records` is fifty, even though thousands sit in the topic. This keeps each batch small enough to score within the poll interval.

Step 3 — the consumer scores each of the up-to-fifty records. Scoring is expensive, but because the batch is bounded, the whole batch finishes well within the five-minute `max.poll.interval.ms`, so the coordinator does not evict the consumer.

Step 4 — only after scoring the whole batch does the consumer call commit-sync. Because auto-commit is off and the commit follows processing, a crash before commit reprocesses the batch rather than losing it, giving at-least-once.

Step 5 — the loop polls again within the interval, so the consumer stays a healthy group member and no rebalance is triggered.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  New group "fraud-scoring", no committed offset
    │
    ▼
  auto.offset.reset = earliest → start at oldest record (read full backlog)
    │
    ▼
  poll() returns AT MOST max.poll.records (50), not the whole topic
    │
    ▼
  score each record (expensive)
    │  must finish + re-poll within max.poll.interval.ms (5 min)
    │  ├─ within interval → stay in group
    │  └─ exceed interval → coordinator evicts → REBALANCE
    ▼
  enable.auto.commit = false → commitSync() AFTER scoring
    │  crash before commit → reprocess (at-least-once, no loss)
    ▼
  loop: poll again within interval → stable membership
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
These four consumer settings control correctness, startup behaviour, and liveness. The auto-commit setting decides whether offsets commit automatically on a timer or manually. The danger of automatic commit is that it can advance the offset past records you have not finished processing, so a crash in that window loses them. So for clean at-least-once I disable auto-commit and call commit only after a batch is fully processed, which means a crash before the commit causes a safe reprocess rather than a loss.

The offset-reset setting only matters when there is no committed offset, such as a brand-new group. Earliest starts at the oldest record so the group reads the whole backlog, which is what you want for a system that must process all history. Latest starts at the end and silently skips everything that already existed, which is a classic reason a brand-new consumer appears to receive nothing. When a committed offset already exists, this setting does nothing because the consumer just resumes.

The max-poll-records setting caps how many records a single poll returns; it is not a total limit and not a byte limit, it just shapes each batch, and I size it down when each record is expensive to process. The max-poll-interval setting bounds the time allowed between successive polls, because polling is how the consumer proves its processing is making progress. If my handler takes longer than that interval, the coordinator assumes I am stuck, evicts me, and triggers a rebalance, which is why a slow handler causes a rebalance even though heartbeats are still flowing.

In my National Bank of India fraud-scoring consumer, I set reset to earliest so it scored the full transaction backlog, disabled auto-commit and committed after scoring so no transaction was ever lost, and because scoring was expensive I lowered max-poll-records so each batch finished well inside the poll interval and the consumer was never evicted mid-batch. Those four settings together gave me a consumer that was complete, safe, and stable.
